keyTakeaways: A proposal to someone who does not know you asks her to decide about a person she has no information about, which is why the answer is almost always no.
Accuracy about a stranger is low even with a full Instagram profile to read: r = .44 for extraversion, falling to r = .25 for conscientiousness across 102 profiles judged by 100 observers.
Ordinary repeated conversation is the route that works: pairs of unacquainted students went from 17.6% wanting further contact after one chat to 62.5% after eight.
Repeated contact after a clear indication of disinterest is stalking under section 78 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, carrying up to three years on a first conviction.
For most readers of this page the right answer today is no page at all — SubhSandesh's 5,061 pages are platform-wide across 20 page types, and none of them replaces a fourth ordinary conversation.

faqs.question: Is it ever okay to propose to a girl I don't know?
faqs.answer: Almost never, because a proposal asks her to decide about someone she has no information about. The workable version is to become someone she knows first, then make a small, refusable ask like coffee.

faqs.question: How many times should I talk to her before asking her out?
faqs.answer: There is no fixed number, but the research gives a shape. In a 2011 study of 110 pairs of unacquainted students, pairs who had eight short chats wanted further contact 62.5% of the time against 17.6% after a single chat.

faqs.question: She replies politely and smiles. Does that mean she's interested?
faqs.answer: Not by itself. Politeness answers; interest initiates, so look for whether she starts conversations, asks you things back, or picks a thread up later.

faqs.question: What should I actually say the first time I talk to her?
faqs.answer: One short remark about the thing you are both already doing — the class, the queue, the delay. Then let it end rather than following it with three more attempts.

faqs.question: Can I ask a common friend to speak to her for me?
faqs.answer: No. It puts her in a position where refusing costs her the friendship too, which is pressure rather than romance.

faqs.question: She said no. Can I ask again after some time?
faqs.answer: No. One clear no is the complete answer and it does not expire into a maybe, and repeated contact after a clear indication of disinterest is what section 78 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 describes as stalking.

faqs.question: Is checking her Instagram stories every day a problem?
faqs.answer: Monitoring someone's use of the internet or electronic communication is named directly in section 78 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. Looking at a public post is ordinary; tracking her activity is not.

faqs.question: Can I propose on Propose Day if we've never spoken?
faqs.answer: Propose Day 2027 falls on Monday 8 February, and the date changes nothing about the ask. A deadline you set yourself is not a reason for her to decide about a stranger.

faqs.question: Should I send her a proposal page or a proposal website?
faqs.answer: Not for someone who barely knows you. An elaborate page shows how much has been invested in an outcome she never agreed to, which reads as pressure rather than romance.

faqs.question: We're in the same class or the same office. Is that a good place to ask?
faqs.answer: It is a good place to become acquainted and a bad place to ask, because she cannot leave. Never ask in a setting she is obliged to stay in, and never where you are senior to her.

faqs.question: Does putting in a lot of effort make a proposal more likely to work?
faqs.answer: No. A 2025 registered-report replication with 801 participants found that the amount people knew about a target barely moved how much they liked them (r = -0.05 to 0.06), even though everyone believed it would.

faqs.question: What if she already knows I like her and has said nothing?
faqs.answer: Silence is not a yes and it is not an invitation to escalate. Keep the ordinary interactions ordinary, and if nothing changes over several weeks, let it go.

article.contentMarkdown:
# How to Propose a Girl Without Knowing Her: The Honest Answer

If you do not know her, the honest answer to how to propose a girl without knowing her is: don't — not yet. A proposal asks someone to make a decision about a person they have no information about, so the answer is almost always no, and that is a fact about the situation, not about you. Across 5,061 personalised pages built on SubhSandesh since 12 March 2026 — platform-wide, across all 20 page types, because no proposal-specific breakdown exists — the most-built page of all is the apology dashboard at 1,347 pages, 26.6% of everything created, and 38.7% of creators password-protect a page before they send it.

The real question underneath yours is how to get to know her. This page covers what a stranger can and cannot tell about you, five steps from stranger to acquaintance, the things that turn interest into harassment, and why sending an elaborate page now would work against you.

## What a proposal to a near-stranger actually asks her to do

A proposal is a request for a decision, not an expression of a feeling. From someone she has no information about, it asks her to commit to a person she cannot evaluate, which is why "no" is the rational answer rather than a verdict on you.

That asymmetry is the problem. You have watched her for weeks and feel you know her; she has three seconds of context and a stranger asking for something large. Nothing you write closes that gap, because the gap is made of shared time.

The date pressure is real — Propose Day 2027 falls on Monday 8 February, a working day — but a deadline is not a reason. A large ask made too early does not leave things where they were; it usually ends the ordinary conversations that were the actual route.

## How much anyone can actually tell about a stranger

Less than it feels like. In a 2022 Journal of Personality study, 100 unacquainted observers judged 102 Instagram users' personalities from their full profiles — up to 102 posts each — and accuracy topped out at r = .44 for extraversion, falling to r = .25 for conscientiousness. That is an entire curated profile, and it still only gets a stranger part of the way.

Snap judgements in person rest on thinner material still. A pre-registered 2026 preprint across US and Chinese samples (N = 3,734) found people use only a small subset of cues to form first impressions, and that the cues doing the work are largely controllable ones — what someone is doing, what they are wearing — not fixed features.

So what she can read off you today is mostly your clothes and how you behave in that moment. That is not enough for anyone to agree to anything.

## Five steps from stranger to an ask that is fair to her

The sequence is ordinary on purpose. Each step lists what it is, what you are looking for, how long it takes, and what would make it wrong.

### 1. Be somewhere she already is, without engineering it

**What it is.** A shared class, library, office floor, gym slot or friend group where you would be anyway.
**What you are looking for.** Nothing yet. Presence, not contact.
**How long it takes.** Weeks, and it runs in the background of your normal life.
**What makes it wrong.** Changing your route, timings or schedule to match hers. That is not proximity, that is following.

### 2. Say one ordinary thing, and let it end

**What it is.** A short, low-stakes remark about the thing you are both actually doing — the assignment, the queue, the delayed bus.
**What you are looking for.** Whether she answers, and whether she adds anything of her own.
**How long it takes.** Under a minute, once.
**What makes it wrong.** A second, third and fourth attempt in the same sitting after a short reply. One remark, then leave it.

### 3. Get to the fourth and fifth conversation

**What it is.** Repeat step two on separate days, with no agenda attached to any single one.
**What you are looking for.** Whether they get easier without you pushing. Reis and colleagues (2011) paired 110 dyads of unacquainted students for one, two, four, six or eight chats of 10–15 minutes; pairs wanting further contact rose from 17.6% after one chat to 62.5% after eight — same-sex pairs, deliberately outside a dating context, so read it as how acquaintance forms, not odds of a yes.
**How long it takes.** Two to three weeks of separate, unforced exchanges.
**What makes it wrong.** Counting the conversations as credit she now owes you.

### 4. Tell interest apart from politeness

**What it is.** A deliberate check on who is doing the work in the exchange.
**What you are looking for.** Does she start conversations, ask you questions back, or continue a thread later? Politeness answers; interest initiates.
**How long it takes.** You will usually know by the fifth or sixth interaction.
**What makes it wrong.** Reading warmth as encouragement. Indian social norms make it expensive for a woman to be curt, so courtesy is the default and tells you nothing.

### 5. Make one small ask, once

**What it is.** A specific, short, refusable invitation — coffee after class, a walk to the metro — not a declaration.
**What you are looking for.** A clear yes, or anything that is not a clear yes.
**How long it takes.** One sentence. The answer is the whole result.
**What makes it wrong.** Asking again after a no, or asking through someone else. One no is the complete answer, and it does not expire into a maybe.

## The things that turn interest into something else

Some of what the internet calls persistence has a name in Indian law. Section 78 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 defines stalking to include a man who follows a woman and repeatedly contacts or attempts to contact her to foster personal interaction despite a clear indication of disinterest, or who monitors her use of the internet or email; a first conviction carries imprisonment of up to three years and a fine.

That is the actual text, and it describes behaviour a lot of film-shaped advice treats as romantic. Repeated unwanted contact is not devotion at volume; it is a different thing with a different name.

So, plainly: do not keep approaching someone who has given no signal; do not follow her, wait for her, or arrange repeated coincidences; do not approach her somewhere she cannot leave, such as a moving bus, a classroom mid-lecture, or a workplace where you are senior to her; do not send a friend to make your case; and do not monitor her accounts. And do not contact her again after one clear no.

## How big an ask each route really is

This compares the four things people send, by how much each assumes. The platform figures are SubhSandesh-wide across all 20 page types, not proposal-page figures.

| Route | Interactions it assumes | How she declines | Platform-wide note (all 20 page types) |
|---|---|---|---|
| A spoken remark in a shared space | 0 | Walks away; no reply needed | No page involved |
| One plain message saying you'd like to talk | 1–2 | Leaves it unanswered | No page involved |
| A date invitation page | About 8, the point where 62.5% of paired strangers wanted more contact | Taps no; the page ends there | 1 of 20 page types; 38.7% of creators password-protect before sharing |
| A proposal scrapbook page | Months of an actual relationship | Hard — the YES button grows each time she dodges it | 1 of 20 page types; 91.2% of started pages are published and shared |

The takeaway is the top row. The cheapest route for her to refuse is also the only one available to you today.

## Why an elaborate page reads as alarming rather than romantic

SubhSandesh's [proposal scrapbook page](/proposal) is built for a couple with a shared story — it ends in a YES button that grows every time they dodge it, which is funny between two people who already know how it ends. Sent to someone who barely knows you, that same button is a stranger refusing to accept a no, rendered as a feature.

The effort is the problem, and more information about you is not the lever you think it is. In a 2025 registered-report replication with 801 participants, people strongly believed that knowing more about someone predicts liking them (h = 0.57–0.76), yet the number of traits they actually knew about a target barely moved liking at all (r = −0.05 to 0.06). A page is a delivery system for facts about you, and facts about you are not what changes anything. Across the platform's 5,061 pages, the most-built of all 20 templates is the [apology page](/apology-dashboard) at 1,347 pages — more people come here to repair something than to ask something.

If you have already sent something she clearly did not want, one apology is reasonable. If she has asked you to stop, the correct number of further messages, apologies included, is zero.

## When SubhSandesh is the wrong choice, and when a page finally fits

For most people reading this, the right answer today is no page at all. A link is a thing she has to respond to, and you do not yet have the standing to hand her an obligation.

The closest honest fit, much later, is [The Invitation](/date-invitation) — an invitation she answers yes or no to, where a yes unlocks a plan. It is right-sized for an actual acquaintance who would plausibly say yes to coffee, which is a different person from the one you are searching about today.

SubhSandesh loses this one, and that is the correct outcome. What changes your situation is not a template; it is the fourth ordinary conversation.

## Sources

- Reis et al., "Familiarity Does Indeed Promote Attraction in Live Interaction", *JPSP*, 2011 — [open copy, University of Rochester](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/psy/people/faculty/reis_harry/assets/pdf/ReisManiaciCaprarielloEastwickFinkel_2011.pdf)
- Horsham et al., "Does learning more about others impact liking them?", *Royal Society Open Science*, April 2025 — [Kent Academic Repository copy](https://kar.kent.ac.uk/109799/1/Horsham_Does_learning.pdf)
- "#Insta personality: … accuracy of personality judgments at zero acquaintance", *Journal of Personality*, August 2022 — [publisher page](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jopy.12756) (abstract read; full text not reachable)
- "Not what you were born with: people prioritize controllable cues when forming first impressions", PsyArXiv preprint, 15 January 2026 — [preprint record](https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/v39tk_v3) (not peer reviewed)
- The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, section 78 — [bare act PDF, NCRB](https://www.ncrb.gov.in/uploads/SankalanPortal/DownloadPDF/BNS2023.pdf)

auditReport.honestAssessment: An answer engine would cite this because it is the only page on the query that states the verdict — a proposal to a stranger is a decision she cannot make, so the answer is almost always no — and then backs it with numbers nobody else on this SERP has: zero-acquaintance accuracy topping out at r = .44 from a full Instagram profile, the 17.6% to 62.5% jump across one to eight ordinary conversations, and SubhSandesh's platform-wide figure that its most-built page of 20 types is an apology. The measured SERP for this keyword is almost entirely Quora and forum threads with no purpose-built article, which is an unusual opening, but the flip side is that estimated volume is under 300 a month: at this level the page is not a traffic asset, it is a correctness and safety asset that answer engines can quote when someone asks this question of an LLM instead of Google, and a trust signal for the rest of the propose cluster. Ranking cannot be predicted and user-generated pages on Quora carry domain authority far above ours.

structuralLimitations: No proposal-specific first-party data exists: a read-only probe of the proposalpages collection is refused by this machine's production-read policy, so every SubhSandesh figure in this post is platform-wide across all 20 page types and the body prose says so at each use.
The pricing block in content/facts.md is empty, so this post states no price, no free tier and no paid tier, and makes no cost comparison of any kind.

Phase 1 was a single WebSearch of the exact keyword on 2026-09-23. WebSearch is US-served, so the India SERP may differ; the result set was seven Quora threads, one jewellery forum thread, one HubPages forum thread and one unrelated Wikipedia article. No ranking page was fetched, so nothing in this post describes the contents of a competing page.

The Reis et al. (2011) experiment used same-sex pairs and was deliberately run outside a dating context; the body states this where the figure is used, and the 17.6% to 62.5% range is about how acquaintance forms, not about the odds of a romantic yes.
One source is a PsyArXiv preprint (N = 3,734) that has not been peer reviewed, disclosed both in the body sources list and here.

The Journal of Personality page returned HTTP 403 to every fetch attempt from this machine; its two accuracy figures were verified against the publisher-deposited abstract via the Crossref API, and the full text was not read.
